entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: From the very beginning of something, such as a job, a project or a relationship.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, interviews and journalism, often to stress that something has been true the whole time: *I knew from day one that she was the one.* With the present perfect, *since day one* is the usual form: *It's been a problem since day one.* It sounds a little more emphatic than *from the start*.
entries.pattern: from day one; since day one (with the present perfect)
examples: Our new boss made it clear **from day one** that she expected everyone at their desks by nine.
My grandparents were crazy about each other **from day one**.
Residents have opposed the new highway ramp **since day one**.

drill.sentence: My roommate and I got along {{from day one}}; by the end of the first week we were cooking dinner together every night.
drill.hint: since the very first moment — a phrase with a number (not *from the start* or *from the get-go*)

entries.related: *from the get-go* — same, more casual; *from the start* — plainer; *from the outset* — more formal, common in writing.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Fixed and final, so that it can no longer be changed.
entries.usage: Mostly used in the negative to say that a plan, date or rule can still change: *Nothing is set in stone yet.* It's common at work and in everyday planning, and it sounds flexible and reassuring. *Written in stone* and *carved in stone* are less common variants.
examples: The wedding date isn't **set in stone**, so let us know if June doesn't work for you.
These are just rough ideas for the new office layout; nothing is **set in stone**.
In my family, Sunday dinner at my parents' house is practically **set in stone**.

drill.sentence: The plan for our camping trip is still flexible — nothing's {{set in stone}} until we book the campsite.
drill.hint: fixed and final, like words cut into rock (the most common form)

entries.related: *written in stone* / *carved in stone* — same, less common; *up in the air* — still undecided; *a done deal* — already agreed and final.

entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: Habits you have had for a long time are very difficult to change or give up.
entries.usage: A short comment, often made with a smile, when someone keeps doing something out of habit even though their situation has changed. It usually explains or excuses the behavior rather than criticizing it. The wording is fixed, and it normally stands as its own sentence or clause.
examples: I retired two years ago, but I still check my work email every morning. **Old habits die hard**.
My dad still saves every plastic bag from the grocery store; **old habits die hard**.
The office switched to a new ticket system months ago, but **old habits die hard**, and half the requests still come in by email.

drill.sentence: Even though I live alone now, I still cook enough pasta for five people. I guess {{old habits die hard}}.
drill.hint: it's difficult to break long-held routines (a saying)

entries.related: *a creature of habit* — a person who likes fixed routines; *you can't teach an old dog new tricks* — older people can't learn new ways, more negative.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A pleasant time spent remembering the past, often prompted by old photos, places, music or people.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, social media posts and feature stories, usually as *take a trip down memory lane* or *be a real trip down memory lane*. It suggests warm nostalgia, not sadness. *A walk down memory lane* is a common variant.
entries.pattern: take a trip down memory lane; be a (real) trip down memory lane
examples: Looking through my mom's old photo albums was a real **trip down memory lane**.
My dad took us on **a trip down memory lane**, pointing out every house he'd lived in as a kid.
For fans who grew up in the nineties, the band's reunion tour is **a trip down memory lane**.

drill.sentence: We found a box of old home videos in the basement and spent the whole evening taking {{a trip down memory lane}}.
drill.hint: a nostalgic journey into the past (not *a walk …*)

entries.related: *a walk down memory lane* — same; *reminisce* — talk or think about pleasant past events; *the good old days* — a past time remembered as better.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A time in the past that people remember as better, simpler or happier than the present.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often with a nostalgic sigh: *Those were the good old days.* It can also be ironic, suggesting the past was not really better: *the good old days of dial-up internet*. The word order is fixed; *the good old times* exists but is much less common.
examples: My uncle loves to talk about **the good old days**, when gas cost thirty cents a gallon.
Some longtime fans miss **the good old days**, when the team played in a small downtown ballpark.
Ah, **the good old days** of waiting twenty minutes for a single photo to download.

drill.sentence: Every time we get together, my college roommates start talking about {{the good old days}} — cheap pizza, no responsibilities and endless free time.
drill.hint: that happier time in the past (with two adjectives)

entries.related: *back in the day* — in the past, casual and less sentimental; *nostalgia* — the feeling of longing for the past; *a trip down memory lane* — a time spent remembering.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something that no longer exists, happens or is used.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, ads and conversation, usually after *be* or *become*: *Paper tickets are becoming a thing of the past.* It can sound positive (a problem is gone) or nostalgic (something good has disappeared). It's often used about technology, habits and problems.
examples: With online banking, writing checks is almost **a thing of the past**.
Thanks to her new medication, my mom's migraines are **a thing of the past**.
In most towns, the corner video store has become **a thing of the past**.

drill.sentence: Since we put in new windows, freezing drafts in the living room are {{a thing of the past}}.
drill.hint: something that no longer happens (not *history*)

entries.related: *history* — informal, as in *That problem is history*; *obsolete* — no longer used because something better exists; *a relic* — an old thing that has survived from the past.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Caught in the act of doing something wrong, so there is no doubt about who did it.
entries.usage: Used about crimes and, humorously, about small wrongs like eating someone else's dessert. The usual patterns are *be caught red-handed* and *catch someone red-handed*. In writing, *red-handed* takes a hyphen.
entries.pattern: be caught red-handed; catch someone red-handed (doing something)
examples: The store's security camera **caught** him **red-handed** slipping a laptop into his backpack.
I **caught** my dog **red-handed** with half a sandwich in her mouth.
Two building inspectors were **caught red-handed** taking cash from a contractor.

drill.sentence: My little brother was caught {{red-handed}} reading my diary when I came home early.
drill.hint: while doing it — a color image (not *in the act*)

entries.related: *caught in the act* — same, plainer; *a smoking gun* — clear proof of guilt; *caught with your hand in the cookie jar* — caught doing something wrong, humorous.
entries.origin: From an older Scottish legal phrase, *with red hand*, used for someone caught with blood still on their hands.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Paid or done secretly, usually in cash, to avoid taxes or rules; also used for illegal payments such as bribes.
entries.usage: Most common with pay and work: *get paid under the table*, *work under the table*. For small cash jobs it suggests avoiding taxes more than serious crime, but *under-the-table payments* often means bribes. Before a noun it takes hyphens: *an under-the-table deal*.
entries.pattern: pay someone / get paid / work under the table; an under-the-table payment
examples: He got paid **under the table** at his uncle's restaurant, so there's no record he ever worked there.
If you pay a roofer **under the table**, you have no warranty when the roof starts leaking.
The report found that the developer had made **under-the-table** payments to win the stadium contract.

drill.sentence: Some landlords want the rent in cash, {{under the table}}, so they don't have to report it as income.
drill.hint: secretly, with no record for taxes — a furniture image (not *off the books*)

entries.related: *off the books* — not recorded officially; *cash in hand* — British for cash wages with no tax; *a kickback* — an illegal payment to someone who helped you get a deal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: So good that it is probably false, a trick or a mistake.
entries.usage: Very common as a warning about offers, deals and news, especially in the saying *If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.* It can also express happy disbelief: *It's almost too good to be true.* It usually follows *sound*, *seem*, *look* or *be*.
examples: A three-bedroom apartment downtown for nine hundred dollars a month? That sounds **too good to be true**.
The job offer seemed **too good to be true**, and it turned out to be a scam.
After years of trying, they're finally expecting a baby — it feels almost **too good to be true**.

drill.sentence: An email says I've won a free cruise, and all I have to do is send my bank details. It's obviously {{too good to be true}}.
drill.hint: so attractive that it can't be real (not *a scam*)

entries.related: *there's no such thing as a free lunch* — nothing valuable is really free; *the catch* — the hidden problem in an offer; *a scam* — a dishonest trick to get money.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Receiving a lot of public attention, often from the media.
entries.usage: Used about people, companies and issues that attract media or public attention. Common patterns are *be in the spotlight*, *put someone in the spotlight* and *step into the spotlight*; the attention can be welcome or unwelcome. *Out of the spotlight* means away from public attention.
examples: After her video went viral, the shy teenager suddenly found herself **in the spotlight**.
The airline has been **in the spotlight** since hundreds of flights were canceled over the holidays.
My brother hates being **in the spotlight**, so we're keeping his birthday party small.

drill.sentence: After winning the state spelling bee, ten-year-old Maya was {{in the spotlight}} for weeks, giving interviews to local TV stations.
drill.hint: the focus of public attention — a stage-light image (not *in the limelight*)

entries.related: *in the public eye* — well known and watched by the public; *in the limelight* — same image, a little old-fashioned; *center stage* — the most important position.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To become well known and respected for your work or skill.
entries.usage: Common in talk about careers, sports and the arts, often with *as* or *in*: *She made a name for herself as a chef.* It suggests success earned through effort over time. The reflexive pronoun matches the subject: *make a name for himself / themselves*.
entries.pattern: make a name for yourself (as + role / in + field)
examples: After years of playing small clubs, the comedian finally **made a name for himself** on late-night TV.
She **made a name for herself** as one of the best pastry chefs in Chicago.
He's a talented young architect who's trying to **make a name for himself** in Boston.

drill.sentence: Before she was famous, the singer {{made a name for herself}} performing in coffee shops all over Nashville.
drill.hint: became well known — the reflexive form, not the one with *mark*

entries.related: *make your name* — same, shorter; *put something on the map* — make a place or thing famous; *a household name* — someone almost everyone has heard of.

entries.term: the light at the end of the tunnel
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Signs that a long, difficult period is finally coming to an end.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and news, usually as *see (the) light at the end of the tunnel* or *there's light at the end of the tunnel*. It's hopeful and is used about illness, debt, long projects and economic crises. A classic joke says the light may be *an oncoming train*.
examples: After eight months of chemo, my aunt can finally see **the light at the end of the tunnel**.
The kitchen remodel has dragged on since March, but there's finally **light at the end of the tunnel**: the countertops arrive Monday.
For farmers hit by three years of drought, this spring's heavy rain finally offers some **light at the end of the tunnel**.

drill.sentence: Our twins are finally sleeping through the night, so after a year of exhaustion we can see {{the light at the end of the tunnel}}.
drill.hint: signs that the hard period is nearly over (an image of a dark passage)

entries.related: *turn a corner* — start to improve after a hard time; *out of the woods* — no longer in danger; *the worst is over* — plain.

entries.term: leave a bad taste in your mouth
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To leave you with an unpleasant feeling, such as disappointment or resentment, after an experience is over.
entries.usage: Used about unfair treatment, rude behavior, or a deal or argument that ended badly: *The whole thing left a bad taste in my mouth.* The subject is usually the experience, and the possessive changes: *in our mouths*, *in everyone's mouth*. *Leave a sour taste* is a common variant.
examples: The way the company announced the layoffs — by email, on a Friday night — **left a bad taste in everyone's mouth**.
We loved the hotel, but a surprise sixty-dollar resort fee at checkout **left a bad taste in our mouths**.
Losing the championship on a disputed call **left a bad taste in** the players' **mouths**.

drill.sentence: The car dealer was friendly until we turned down the extended warranty, and his sudden rudeness {{left a bad taste in my mouth}}.
drill.hint: gave me an unpleasant feeling afterward (a flavor image; not the *sour* version)

entries.related: *leave a sour taste* — same; *rub someone the wrong way* — irritate someone through your manner; *sour on something* — start to dislike it.

entries.term: in one ear and out the other
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Heard but immediately forgotten or ignored, without having any effect.
entries.usage: Usually *go in one ear and out the other*, a complaint from parents, teachers and partners about someone who doesn't listen. The subject is the thing that was said: *Everything I say goes in one ear and out the other.* It's informal and often humorous.
entries.pattern: something goes in one ear and out the other
examples: I've told my son a hundred times to hang up his coat, but it goes **in one ear and out the other**.
The flight attendant's safety talk went **in one ear and out the other**; I was too excited about the trip.
Be honest — did anything I said in that meeting stick, or was it all **in one ear and out the other**?

drill.sentence: I reminded my teenager about his curfew three times tonight, and I'm sure it went {{in one ear and out the other}}.
drill.hint: was heard and instantly forgotten (an image of passing through someone's head)

entries.related: *fall on deaf ears* — be ignored, more formal; *tune someone out* — stop listening to someone; *not sink in* — not be understood or remembered.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An advantage you have over others from the beginning, often because you started earlier.
entries.usage: Common in education, sports, careers and business: *get a head start on something*, *give someone a head start*. It's neutral and often used to recommend starting early: *Let's get a head start on the packing.* *Head start* is written as two words.
entries.pattern: get / have / give someone a head start (on / over someone or something)
examples: Kids who learn to read at home often get **a head start** in kindergarten.
Let's leave at five to get **a head start** on the holiday traffic.
The startup had a two-year **head start** on its competitors and grabbed most of the market.

drill.sentence: Her parents read to her every night, which gave her {{a head start}} over the other kids in first grade.
drill.hint: an advantage from beginning earlier than others (not *an edge* or *a leg up*)

entries.related: *an edge* — any advantage, not only from starting early; *get a jump on something* — start early, informal American; *a level playing field* — a fair situation with no advantage for anyone.

entries.term: take matters into your own hands
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deal with a problem yourself because the people responsible have not done anything about it.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, and it often shows frustration with officials, companies or other people who failed to act. It can sound positive (taking initiative) or worrying, when people act outside the law. The possessive matches the subject: *They took matters into their own hands.*
examples: After the city ignored their complaints for months, residents **took matters into their own hands** and painted a crosswalk themselves.
Tired of waiting for the landlord, I **took matters into my own hands** and fixed the leaky faucet.
Police warned shoppers not to **take matters into their own hands** if they see a shoplifter.

drill.sentence: The airline kept making excuses about our lost suitcase, so my mom {{took matters into her own hands}} and drove to the airport to find it.
drill.hint: dealt with it personally because nobody else would

entries.related: *take charge* — assume control of a situation; *take the law into your own hands* — punish someone yourself, illegally; *take the initiative* — act first without being told.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make no effort at all to help, especially when help is clearly needed.
entries.usage: Always negative: *didn't lift a finger*, *never lifts a finger*, *won't lift a finger*, often followed by *to help* or *to* + verb. It's a complaint about lazy or unhelpful people, common in talk about housework, family and coworkers.
entries.pattern: not / never lift a finger (to help / to do something)
examples: I cooked Thanksgiving dinner for twelve people, and my brothers **didn't lift a finger** to help.
My roommate **never lifts a finger** around the apartment.
The company **won't lift a finger** to fix the problem unless customers start complaining publicly.

drill.sentence: Mark talks a lot about protecting the park, but when we organized the cleanup, he {{didn't lift a finger}}.
drill.hint: made no effort at all to help (a hand image)

mistake.wrong: He didn't move a finger to help us.
mistake.right: He didn't lift a finger to help us.
mistake.why: The English verb is *lift*; *move a finger* is a word-for-word translation from languages like German, Spanish or Italian.

entries.related: *sit on your hands* — fail to act when you should; *pull your weight* — do your fair share, the opposite; *do nothing* — plain.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Already achieved or experienced, in a way that will help you in the future.
entries.usage: Used with *have*, *get* or *with*, often with numbers: *with ten years of teaching under her belt*. It's common in job talk, sports and travel, and stresses that the experience is useful. The possessive changes: *under his belt*, *under our belts*.
entries.pattern: have / get something under your belt; with + experience + under your belt
examples: With two marathons **under her belt**, she's ready to try an ultramarathon.
It's good to have a few short trips **under your belt** before you backpack across Asia alone.
The new store manager has fifteen years of retail experience **under his belt**.

drill.sentence: Now that he has a full season {{under his belt}}, the young quarterback looks much more confident.
drill.hint: already done, as useful experience — a clothing image (not *behind him*)

entries.related: *behind you* — finished, often something hard you're glad is over; *a track record* — a record of past results; *a seasoned pro* — someone with a lot of experience.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have a secret plan, idea or trick ready to use when the time is right.
entries.usage: Common in questions and predictions, as in *What does she have up her sleeve?* or *He's got a few tricks up his sleeve.* It's light and often playful, used about surprises, competitors and negotiations. *An ace up your sleeve* is a hidden advantage you can use at the right moment.
entries.pattern: have something / a trick or two / an ace up your sleeve
examples: The coach always has a trick or two **up his sleeve** for the playoffs.
From the way my wife was smiling, I could tell she **had something up her sleeve** for my birthday.
Analysts are wondering what the phone maker **has up its sleeve** for its fall launch.

drill.sentence: Don't count Ellen out of the chess tournament yet; I'm sure she {{has something up her sleeve}}.
drill.hint: has a secret plan ready (a magician's image)

entries.related: *an ace up your sleeve* — a hidden advantage; *keep something under wraps* — keep a plan secret; *a trick or two* — a few clever ideas.

entries.term: stand on your own two feet
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be independent and support yourself, especially financially, without help from your parents or others.
entries.usage: Common in talk about young adults leaving home, people starting over and new businesses. It's positive and often describes what parents hope for: *learn to stand on your own two feet*. *Two* is usually included, and the possessive matches the subject.
examples: My parents paid for college, but after graduation they expected me to **stand on my own two feet**.
The program helps young people leaving foster care **stand on their own two feet**.
The bakery needed help from investors at first, but now it **stands on its own two feet**.

drill.sentence: Moving across the country for my first job taught me to {{stand on my own two feet}}.
drill.hint: be independent and support myself (a body image)

entries.related: *get back on your feet* — recover after a hard time; *fend for yourself* — take care of yourself without help; *leave the nest* — move out of your parents' home.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Praise or approval for something you have done well.
entries.usage: Common at work, at school and in sports: *give someone a pat on the back*, *deserve a pat on the back*. *Give yourself a pat on the back* is a friendly way to congratulate someone. It can also sound small, as in *All I got was a pat on the back*, meaning praise instead of a real reward.
examples: You all deserve **a pat on the back** for finishing the project early.
Give yourself **a pat on the back** — you've stuck to your workout plan for a whole month.
After twenty years of overtime, all he got was **a pat on the back** and a gift card.

drill.sentence: The volunteers who cleaned up the beach after the storm deserve {{a pat on the back}}.
drill.hint: praise for a job well done — a friendly gesture (not *a round of applause*)

entries.related: *kudos* — praise, informal; *a round of applause* — public praise, often literal clapping; *pat yourself on the back* — feel proud of yourself, sometimes too proud.

entries.term: have a good head on your shoulders
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be sensible and practical and to have good judgment.
entries.usage: Usually said with approval by older people about younger ones: *She has a good head on her shoulders.* It stresses common sense and good decisions more than brilliance. The possessive matches the subject, and *has got* is common in speech: *He's got a good head on his shoulders.*
examples: I'm not worried about our daughter moving to New York; she **has a good head on her shoulders**.
Hire Daniel — he's young, but he's **got a good head on his shoulders**.
Her parents gave her a lot of freedom because she clearly **had a good head on her shoulders**.

drill.sentence: Don't worry about Jake handling the money for the trip; he {{has a good head on his shoulders}}.
drill.hint: is sensible and practical (a body image; not the *screwed on* version)

entries.related: *level-headed* — calm and sensible; *street-smart* — good at handling real-life situations; *have your head in the clouds* — be unrealistic, the opposite.

entries.term: have a bone to pick with someone
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To have a complaint that you want to discuss with someone, usually about something they did.
entries.usage: Usually an opening line, half-joking or serious: *I have a bone to pick with you.* It warns the listener that a complaint is coming. It's informal and used between friends, family and coworkers; *I've got a bone to pick with you* is common in speech.
examples: **I've got a bone to pick with you** — why did you tell Mom about my new tattoo?
My neighbor knocked on the door this morning because she **had a bone to pick with** me about my leaves blowing into her yard.
Many fans **have a bone to pick with** the league over the new ticket prices.

drill.sentence: Hey, I {{have a bone to pick with you}}: who ate the leftover lasagna I was saving for lunch?
drill.hint: want to complain to you about something (a dog image)

entries.related: *take something up with someone* — raise a complaint, often formally; *have it out with someone* — have an open argument to settle a problem; *a sore point* — a topic that upsets someone.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be so beautiful or impressive that you feel amazed for a moment.
entries.usage: Used about views, art, music, performances and beautiful people: *The view took my breath away.* It's emotional and positive, and the subject is the thing that impresses you. The adjective *breathtaking* comes from the same image.
examples: The view from the rim of the Grand Canyon **took my breath away**.
When she walked down the aisle in her wedding dress, she **took his breath away**.
The cellist's solo was so beautiful that it **took the audience's breath away**.

drill.sentence: The first time I saw the northern lights in Alaska, the colors {{took my breath away}}.
drill.hint: amazed me so much that I almost stopped breathing

entries.related: *blow someone away* — impress someone hugely, more casual; *breathtaking* — extremely beautiful; *jaw-dropping* — shockingly impressive.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said when the person you have just been talking about appears or calls.
entries.usage: A light, friendly remark, often said with a laugh as the person walks in: *Speak of the devil — here she is!* It isn't an insult, so you can use it about friends and coworkers. The longer form, *speak of the devil and he shall appear*, is rare in everyday speech.
examples: We were just wondering where Tom was — **speak of the devil**, here he comes.
"Has anyone heard from Jen lately?" Just then my phone buzzed. "**Speak of the devil**!"
**Speak of the devil**! We were just talking about your new job.

drill.sentence: "I bet Carlos forgot about the barbecue." The doorbell rang, and there he was. "{{Speak of the devil}}!"
drill.hint: said when the person you were discussing shows up (the usual American form)

entries.related: *talk of the devil* — same, more common in British English; *your ears must be burning* — said to someone who was just being talked about.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To spoil someone's plans or happy moment, often by pointing out a problem.
entries.usage: Very common as an apology before bad news: *I hate to rain on your parade, but…* It's informal and usually friendly in tone. The possessive changes: *rain on my parade*, *rain on everyone's parade*.
examples: I hate to **rain on your parade**, but the beach house you booked doesn't allow dogs.
My sister was thrilled about her new car until Dad **rained on her parade** by asking about the insurance.
Don't let one bad review **rain on your parade**; opening night was a huge success.

drill.sentence: I don't want to {{rain on your parade}}, but the concert tickets you bought are for next year, not this Saturday.
drill.hint: spoil your happy moment — a weather image (not *burst your bubble*)

entries.related: *burst someone's bubble* — destroy someone's happy belief; *a wet blanket* — a person who spoils other people's fun; *buzzkill* — slang for a person or thing that spoils the fun.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To become very successful or popular very quickly in a place or with a group of people.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and marketing about performers, products and trends: *take the world / the city / the internet by storm*. It's positive and slightly dramatic. The object is the place or audience that is won over, not the product.
examples: Pickleball has **taken** the country **by storm**, and new courts are popping up everywhere.
The young pianist **took** New York **by storm** with her first concert at Carnegie Hall.
When the taco truck arrived last summer, it **took** our little town **by storm**.

drill.sentence: K-pop has {{taken the world by storm}}, with sold-out stadium tours from Los Angeles to London.
drill.hint: become hugely popular very quickly (a weather image)

entries.related: *catch on* — become popular, plainer; *go viral* — spread quickly online; *an overnight success* — a success that seems to come suddenly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To respond to an attack or a problem by using the same methods your opponent is using.
entries.usage: Used in competition, business, sports and arguments, often to justify tough tactics: *We have to fight fire with fire.* It can sound approving, but people also use it to warn that matching bad behavior only makes things worse. The form is fixed.
examples: When the rival store started cutting prices, we decided to **fight fire with fire**.
If a bully insults you, **fighting fire with fire** usually just makes things worse.
Their lawyers buried us in paperwork, so we **fought fire with fire** and did the same to them.

drill.sentence: The other team kept playing rough, so our captain told us to {{fight fire with fire}} and stop backing down.
drill.hint: use the same tough methods as the other side (a flame image)

entries.related: *give someone a taste of their own medicine* — treat someone as badly as they treated you; *tit for tat* — an equal action in return, often petty; *turn the other cheek* — not respond to an attack, the opposite.

entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: Both people involved in a situation, especially a conflict or a relationship, share the responsibility for it.
entries.usage: Used to point out that blame should be shared, often in arguments, breakups and scandals: *Don't blame only him; it takes two to tango.* It's informal and slightly humorous. It also works for cooperation, when an agreement needs both sides to want it.
examples: Sure, he started the argument, but **it takes two to tango** — you kept yelling too.
The tabloids blamed the singer for the breakup, but **it takes two to tango**.
A trade deal can't work if only one country wants it; **it takes two to tango**.

drill.sentence: Mom punished only my brother for the fight, but I told her, "{{It takes two to tango}} — I was just as guilty."
drill.hint: both people share the blame (a dance image)

entries.related: *share the blame* — plain; *six of one, half a dozen of the other* — both sides are equally responsible; *a two-way street* — a situation that needs effort from both sides.
entries.origin: Popularized by the 1952 American song *Takes Two to Tango*.

entries.term: out of sight, out of mind
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: People soon forget about things or people that they no longer see regularly.
entries.usage: Used both as an explanation for forgetting and as a deliberate strategy, such as hiding snacks so you eat fewer of them. It's also a common worry in long-distance relationships and remote work. The form is fixed, and it usually stands alone after a dash or a comma.
examples: I put the candy on the top shelf — **out of sight, out of mind**.
Once my college friends moved away, it was **out of sight, out of mind**, and we slowly stopped calling.
Many remote workers worry that when promotions come around, it'll be **out of sight, out of mind**.

drill.sentence: I keep my credit card in a drawer at home instead of in my wallet. {{Out of sight, out of mind}}.
drill.hint: what you don't see, you forget about (a saying)

entries.related: *absence makes the heart grow fonder* — the opposite saying: missing someone makes you love them more; *lose touch* — stop being in contact.

entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: The way you treat other people will eventually come back to you, whether good or bad.
entries.usage: Usually said about someone who behaved badly and later suffered for it, sometimes with a little satisfaction. It can also be a warning, or a reason to be kind. The form is fixed and it usually stands alone as a sentence.
examples: He cheated his business partners for years, and now he's being sued. **What goes around comes around**.
Be nice to people on your way up — **what goes around comes around**.
The neighbor who kept calling the police about our parties just got a noise complaint himself. **What goes around comes around**!

drill.sentence: My cousin was rude to every waiter he met, and now he's waiting tables himself. I guess {{what goes around comes around}}.
drill.hint: how you treat others returns to you (a saying)

entries.related: *karma* — the idea that your actions come back to you; *you reap what you sow* — your actions bring the results you deserve, more formal; *get your just deserts* — get the punishment you deserve.

entries.term: if it ain't broke, don't fix it
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: Don't change something that already works well, because the change may only cause problems.
entries.usage: A folksy American saying used at work and in everyday life against unnecessary changes. *Ain't* and *broke* are deliberately nonstandard, and the saying is still fine in professional conversation. It's often shortened to *if it ain't broke…*, and some writers prefer *if it isn't broken, don't fix it*.
examples: Our billing software is twenty years old, but it works. **If it ain't broke, don't fix it**.
The new owners changed the diner's famous menu and lost half their regulars. Clearly nobody told them **if it ain't broke, don't fix it**.
My neighbor has fished the same spot for forty years; his motto is "**If it ain't broke, don't fix it**."

drill.sentence: My mom has used the same pancake recipe for thirty years. When I suggested adding bananas, she said, "{{If it ain't broke, don't fix it}}."
drill.hint: leave alone what already works well (a folksy saying)

entries.related: *leave well enough alone* — don't try to improve something that is fine; *don't rock the boat* — don't cause trouble by changing things.
entries.origin: Popularized in 1977 by Bert Lance, a US federal budget official.

entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: A simpler approach, with fewer things or less detail, is often more effective.
entries.usage: Common in design, writing, cooking, fashion and presentations as advice against overdoing things. It sounds wise and is often used to justify cutting something. It usually stands alone or follows *believe* or *remember*.
examples: When you give a toast at a wedding, **less is more**: three minutes is plenty.
The chef believes **less is more**, so most of her dishes have only four or five ingredients.
Your slides are way too crowded. Remember, **less is more**.

drill.sentence: I used to cover every wall with pictures, but now I think {{less is more}} — the room feels calmer with just one painting.
drill.hint: simplicity works better (a three-word saying)

entries.related: *keep it simple* — plain advice; *overkill* — far more than is needed; *minimalism* — a style that uses very few elements.
entries.origin: It appears in an 1855 poem by Robert Browning and later became a motto of the architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe.

entries.term: fake it till you make it
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: Act confident and capable, even if you don't feel that way yet, until you really become confident or successful.
entries.usage: Common American advice about new jobs, public speaking and shyness, usually meant as encouragement. It can also be critical, about people who pretend to have skills or results they don't really have. *Till*, *'til* and *until* all appear in writing.
examples: My advice for your first big presentation? **Fake it till you make it**.
She had never managed a team before, but she **faked it till she made it**, and now she runs the whole department.
Critics say some startup founders take **fake it till you make it** too far and mislead investors about their products.

drill.sentence: If you feel shy at parties, try to {{fake it till you make it}}: smile, ask questions and act like you're having fun.
drill.hint: act confident until you really are (a rhyming saying)

entries.related: *put on a brave face* — hide fear or sadness; *impostor syndrome* — the feeling that you don't deserve your success; *look the part* — seem right for a role.

entries.term: don't judge a book by its cover
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: Don't judge someone or something only by appearance, because the appearance can be misleading.
entries.usage: Very common advice about people, places and things, often said after a pleasant surprise. *You can't judge a book by its cover* is just as common as the imperative form. It's neutral and fits almost any conversation.
examples: The restaurant looks like a dump from the outside, but **don't judge a book by its cover** — the food is amazing.
My new coworker seemed cold at first, but **you can't judge a book by its cover**; she's actually really kind.
That beat-up old pickup has the best engine on the lot — **never judge a book by its cover**.

drill.sentence: The old man in muddy overalls turned out to own the whole ranch. You really can't {{judge a book by its cover}}.
drill.hint: decide what something is like from how it looks (a reading image)

entries.related: *looks can be deceiving* — appearances may be false; *more than meets the eye* — more complex or interesting than it seems; *first impressions* — early opinions, often based on appearance.

entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: What people do shows their real intentions and feelings better than what they say.
entries.usage: Used to criticize empty promises or to encourage people to show their feelings through what they do: *He says he's sorry, but actions speak louder than words.* It's neutral and common in relationships, sports and business. The form is fixed.
examples: He keeps saying he'll help more around the house, but **actions speak louder than words**.
Instead of telling your team you value them, give them a raise. **Actions speak louder than words**.
Our principal doesn't give big speeches; she believes **actions speak louder than words**.

drill.sentence: Don't just tell your sister you're sorry — show up at her recital. {{Actions speak louder than words}}.
drill.hint: deeds matter more; promises are cheap (a saying)

entries.related: *walk the walk* — act on what you say; *all talk and no action* — making promises but doing nothing; *put your money where your mouth is* — support your words with action or money.

entries.term: the grass is always greener on the other side
entries.label: saying
entries.meaning: Other people's situations always seem better than your own, even when they are not.
entries.usage: Used as a warning to someone who wants to change jobs, partners or places because they think life will be better elsewhere. It's very often shortened to *the grass is always greener*, and the long form sometimes ends *…on the other side of the fence*. It's neutral and common in conversation and advice columns.
examples: You keep looking at other jobs, but remember, **the grass is always greener on the other side**.
My city friends envy my quiet life in the country, and I envy their nightlife; **the grass is always greener on the other side**.
Parents of toddlers envy parents of teenagers, and the other way around — **the grass is always greener**.

drill.sentence: My brother left his small town for New York and now dreams of moving back; {{the grass is always greener on the other side}}, I guess.
drill.hint: someone else's life looks better from far away (a lawn image)

entries.related: *the grass is greener where you water it* — a modern reply: improve your own situation instead; *be careful what you wish for* — a desired change may bring problems.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To spread very quickly to many people or places.
entries.usage: Used about news, rumors, trends and sometimes diseases: *The rumor spread like wildfire.* It's common in journalism and conversation and stresses speed and lack of control. For online content, people also say that it *went viral*.
examples: News of the layoffs **spread like wildfire** through the office.
The video **spread like wildfire** online, and by morning it had ten million views.
In a small town, gossip **spreads like wildfire**.

drill.sentence: When the principal announced a snow day, the news {{spread like wildfire}}, and within minutes every kid in town was outside.
drill.hint: traveled extremely fast — a fire image (not *went viral*)

entries.related: *go viral* — spread quickly online; *the word got out* — the news became known; *snowball* — grow quickly and become harder to control.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To correct a false story, rumor or wrong idea by giving the true facts.
entries.usage: Common in news, interviews, public statements and conversation, often after rumors or misreporting: *I'd like to set the record straight.* It sounds firm and slightly formal. It's often followed by *on* or *about* + topic.
entries.pattern: set the record straight (on / about something)
examples: The actor posted a video to **set the record straight** about the rumors of his divorce.
Let me **set the record straight**: I never said the plan was a bad idea.
A retired history teacher wrote to the local newspaper to **set the record straight** on the history of the old mill.

drill.sentence: People keep saying the new café is owned by a big chain, so the owner put up a sign to {{set the record straight}}.
drill.hint: correct the false story — a phrase about the official account (not *clear things up*)

entries.related: *clear the air* — talk openly to end tension or a misunderstanding; *clear things up* — explain to remove confusion; *for the record* — said before stating something officially.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To perform well when a difficult or important situation demands it, often better than people expected.
entries.usage: Used as praise for people who do well under pressure: in sports, emergencies, exams or public speaking. It's neutral and fits both speech and writing. The negative is *fail to rise to the occasion*.
examples: Nobody expected much from the backup goalie, but he **rose to the occasion** and stopped every shot.
When my dad got sick, my younger brother really **rose to the occasion** and took care of everything.
Big crowds make some performers nervous, but she always **rises to the occasion**.

drill.sentence: The young cook had to feed two hundred guests when the head chef got sick, and she {{rose to the occasion}}.
drill.hint: performed well under pressure (not *stepped up* or *came through*)

entries.related: *step up* — take responsibility when it's needed; *clutch* — performing well in key moments, American sports slang; *crack under pressure* — fail because of stress, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To solve a problem at the last moment and prevent failure or disaster.
entries.usage: Used about a person or a thing that rescues a situation, often humorously and about small problems: *Your phone charger saved the day.* It's common in conversation, sports and news. The subject can be a person or an object.
examples: The caterer canceled at the last minute, but my neighbor **saved the day** with three trays of enchiladas.
A roll of duct tape **saved the day** when our car's bumper started falling off on the highway.
The rookie's goal in the final seconds **saved the day** for the home team.

drill.sentence: We forgot the tent poles on our camping trip, but a friendly family at the next site {{saved the day}} by lending us theirs.
drill.hint: rescued us from disaster (not *came to the rescue*)

entries.related: *come to the rescue* — help someone in trouble; *a lifesaver* — a person or thing that helps at a crucial moment, informal; *in the nick of time* — at the last possible moment.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To help, teach and protect someone who has less experience than you.
entries.usage: Common in talk about work, school and sports, about mentors and older colleagues. It's warm and positive. The possessive matches the helper: *She took me under her wing.*
examples: When I started at the hospital, an older nurse **took me under her wing** and showed me how everything worked.
The team captain **took** the nervous rookie **under his wing**.
Mrs. Lopez next door **took** half the kids on our block **under her wing**; they all ate dinner at her place.

drill.sentence: The new kid in class didn't know anyone, so my daughter {{took him under her wing}} and introduced him to her friends.
drill.hint: looked after and guided him (a bird image)

entries.related: *mentor* — guide a less experienced person, more formal; *show someone the ropes* — teach a newcomer the basics; *look out for someone* — protect someone's interests.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To act in a fair, honest and dignified way, especially when others are behaving badly toward you.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, advice and news, often when someone chooses not to answer insults or attacks: *I decided to take the high road.* It's approving. *Take the low road* is the opposite: to respond in a mean or dishonest way.
examples: My ex said some nasty things about me online, but I **took the high road** and didn't respond.
After the close loss, the coach **took the high road** and praised the other team instead of blaming the referees.
It's tempting to write an angry review, but **taking the high road** usually feels better in the long run.

drill.sentence: When her sister-in-law criticized her cooking at Thanksgiving, Lisa {{took the high road}} and simply thanked everyone for coming.
drill.hint: stayed dignified instead of hitting back — a route image (not *rose above it*)

entries.related: *rise above something* — not let something bad affect you; *be the bigger person* — be the one who forgives or stays calm; *stoop to someone's level* — behave as badly as they do.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To work very well or exactly as intended, often quickly or surprisingly easily.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and online reviews about tips, tricks, fixes and home remedies: *The vinegar trick worked like a charm.* It's informal and positive, and usually in the past tense after trying something. The form is fixed.
examples: I poured baking soda and vinegar down the clogged drain, and it **worked like a charm**.
The new bedtime routine **worked like a charm**; the baby now sleeps until six.
The shortcut Maria suggested **worked like a charm**, and we beat the traffic home.

drill.sentence: My roommate's honey-and-lemon remedy {{worked like a charm}}, and my cough was gone in two days.
drill.hint: was perfectly effective, as if by a magic spell (not *did the trick* or *… wonders*)

entries.related: *work wonders* — have a very good effect; *do the trick* — achieve what is needed, more casual; *backfire* — have the opposite effect.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The result of chance, not of skill or choice.
entries.usage: Used to accept a result you couldn't control, often with a shrug: *It's just the luck of the draw.* It's common about schedules, assignments, seating, weather and sports draws. It usually follows *it's* or *that's*.
examples: Which teacher your kid gets is really just **the luck of the draw**.
We got the worst campsite, right next to the bathrooms, but that's **the luck of the draw**.
By **the luck of the draw**, our team faced the defending champions in the first round.

drill.sentence: Some years we get a mild winter and some years we get three feet of snow; it's just {{the luck of the draw}}.
drill.hint: decided by chance alone (a card-game image)

entries.related: *a roll of the dice* — something risky that depends on chance; *hit or miss* — sometimes good, sometimes bad; *fate* — events seen as decided in advance.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To accept something unpleasant, such as a boring task or a personal sacrifice, so that the group benefits.
entries.usage: Informal and often humorous, used about chores, bad seats, dull meetings or babysitting: *I'll take one for the team.* It can be sincere or sarcastic. The form is fixed.
examples: Nobody wanted to work on Christmas Eve, so I **took one for the team**.
Fine, I'll **take one for the team** and sit next to Uncle Bob at dinner.
Several players **took one for the team** and accepted smaller contracts so the club could sign a star.

drill.sentence: Someone has to stay sober and drive everyone home after the party, so I guess I'll {{take one for the team}}.
drill.hint: make a personal sacrifice for the group (a sports image)

entries.related: *bite the bullet* — do something unpleasant that can't be avoided; *fall on your sword* — accept blame to protect others; *for the greater good* — for the benefit of the group.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Extremely high or extremely good, far beyond the normal range.
entries.usage: Common in American speech, ads and sports talk about numbers, energy, talent or emotions: *Her energy is off the charts.* It can describe measurable data, such as blood pressure or sales, or simply express enthusiasm. Before a noun it's hyphenated: *off-the-charts demand*.
examples: Demand for the new game console has been **off the charts** since it launched.
The doctor said my cholesterol was **off the charts** and put me on a strict diet.
The energy in the stadium during the final was **off the charts**.

drill.sentence: Our new puppy's energy is {{off the charts}}; he runs laps around the yard at five in the morning.
drill.hint: extremely high — a graph image (not *through the roof*)

entries.related: *through the roof* — very high after rising quickly; *sky-high* — very high, especially prices; *out of this world* — extremely good.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Available for anyone who wants to try to get it or win it.
entries.usage: Used about prizes, jobs, titles, seats, leftover food and free items: *There are two tickets up for grabs.* It's informal and suggests competition or a first-come, first-served chance. In sports, it often means the result is still open.
examples: Our manager is retiring in June, and her job is **up for grabs**.
With three games left, the division title is still **up for grabs**.
We're giving away our old couch; it's **up for grabs** if you can pick it up this weekend.

drill.sentence: The last slice of birthday cake is {{up for grabs}} if anyone still wants it.
drill.hint: free for whoever takes it first (a reaching image)

entries.related: *first come, first served* — given in the order people arrive; *anyone's game* — a contest that anyone could still win; *on the table* — available for discussion.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Exactly the kind of thing someone likes, is interested in or is good at.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, especially when recommending something: *This book is right up your alley.* It's warm and informal. *Up your alley* without *right* is also used, and British English prefers *right up your street*.
examples: You love history and old houses, so this walking tour is **right up your alley**.
A job testing video games? That's **right up my alley**.
The new barbecue place downtown sounds **right up** Dad's **alley**.

drill.sentence: My brother loves spicy food and long hikes, so a trip to New Mexico is {{right up his alley}}.
drill.hint: exactly what he enjoys — the American form (not *his cup of tea*)

entries.related: *right up your street* — British version; *your cup of tea* — something you like, often negative: *not my cup of tea*; *your thing* — something you enjoy, casual.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very annoyed and bored with something because it has happened or continued for too long.
entries.usage: A strong, informal complaint, often about someone's repeated behavior: *I'm sick and tired of cleaning up after you.* It's followed by a noun or an *-ing* form. It's stronger than *tired of* and often sounds angry.
entries.pattern: be sick and tired of + noun / -ing
examples: I'm **sick and tired of** hearing excuses about why the rent is late.
Residents are **sick and tired of** the noise from the construction site next door.
She was **sick and tired of** her two-hour commute, so she found a job closer to home.

drill.sentence: I'm {{sick and tired of}} finding dirty dishes in the sink every morning!
drill.hint: really annoyed by — a phrase with two adjectives (not *fed up with*)

mistake.wrong: I'm sick and tired to wait for the bus every morning.
mistake.right: I'm sick and tired of waiting for the bus every morning.
mistake.why: *Sick and tired* is followed by *of* + a noun or an *-ing* form, not by an infinitive.

entries.related: *fed up with* — very annoyed by, slightly milder; *have had it with* — can no longer accept something; *at the end of your rope* — so frustrated you can't cope.
